gloss: The open ground behind a house, often fenced.
examples: The kids are out in the *backyard*.
We grilled in the *backyard* until it got dark.
Most of the *backyards* on this street back onto the creek.
contrast: Americans say *backyard*; the British say back garden.

gloss: The piece of ground between a house and the street.
examples: He was out mowing the *front yard* at seven in the morning.
There's a big maple in the *front yard*.
All the *front yards* on the block are watered by timer.

gloss: A long flexible tube for carrying water to a lawn or garden.
examples: Roll up the *garden hose* before somebody trips on it.
The *garden hose* is leaking right at the connector.
We keep two *garden hoses*, one front and one back.

gloss: A plot of ground where food plants are grown.
examples: They put in a *vegetable garden* along the south fence.
Half the *vegetable garden* is tomatoes.
*Vegetable gardens* need at least six hours of sun.
contrast: Russian огород is a *vegetable garden*; plain *garden* in American English usually means the flowers and shrubs.

gloss: A planting box of soil built up above the level of the ground.
examples: He built a *raised bed* out of cedar boards.
The lettuce goes in the shady *raised bed*.
Four *raised beds* fit easily in that yard.

gloss: The work of pulling unwanted plants out of a garden.
examples: I spent all Saturday morning *weeding*.
*Weeding* is easier right after a rain.
There's a lot of *weeding* to do out back.

gloss: The cutting back of branches or stems to shape a plant or help it grow.
examples: The apple trees need *pruning* before the buds swell.
Heavy *pruning* in fall can hurt a young tree.
She does all her *pruning* in late winter.

gloss: The act of putting seeds or young plants into the ground.
examples: The soil is still too cold for *planting*.
He got the *planting* done in one weekend.
Water the bed well after *planting*.

gloss: The cutting of grass to keep a lawn short.
examples: *Mowing* takes him about an hour.
The lawn needs *mowing* twice a week in June.
I hired a kid down the street to do the *mowing*.

gloss: The giving of water to plants.
examples: Early morning is the best time for *watering*.
The pots need *watering* every single day in August.
Can you take over the *watering* while we're gone?

gloss: The work of gathering leaves or smoothing soil with a rake.
examples: *Raking* leaves is a whole weekend around here.
My shoulders are sore from all that *raking*.
The yard still needs one more round of *raking*.

gloss: The scattering or setting of seed in prepared ground.
examples: Direct *sowing* works fine for beans and squash.
The packet gives a *sowing* depth of half an inch.
*Sowing* too early usually costs you the whole crop.
contrast: *Sowing* rhymes with going; the *sow* that means a female pig rhymes with cow.

gloss: The spreading of bark, straw, or leaves over soil to hold moisture in.
examples: *Mulching* cuts my watering in half.
We finished the *mulching* on Sunday afternoon.
Heavy *mulching* keeps the weeds from coming up.

gloss: The practice of letting plant waste rot down into food for the soil.
examples: The city has a class on backyard *composting*.
*Composting* got rid of most of our kitchen trash.
She's been *composting* for twenty years.

gloss: The regular work of feeding, cutting, and watering a lawn.
examples: They pay a service for *lawn care*.
*Lawn care* around here means watering three times a week.
He knows more about *lawn care* than anyone on the block.

gloss: Outdoor chores like mowing, raking, and trimming around a house.
examples: I've got a ton of *yard work* this weekend.
He does *yard work* to stay out of the house.
Saturday is for *yard work* and nothing else.

gloss: Grass, leaves, and branches thrown out after garden work.
examples: *Yard waste* goes in the green bin.
The town picks up *yard waste* on Thursdays.
We had six bags of *yard waste* after the storm.

gloss: A closed container where plant scraps are left to rot into compost.
examples: Coffee grounds go straight into the *compost bin*.
The *compost bin* is behind the garage.
We run two *compost bins* so one can finish.

gloss: A heap of rotting plant material kept for feeding the soil.
examples: Throw those weeds on the *compost pile*.
The *compost pile* steams on cold mornings.
He turns the *compost pile* with a pitchfork every few weeks.

gloss: The dark upper layer of soil where most plant roots grow.
examples: The builders scraped off all the *topsoil*.
We had a truckload of *topsoil* delivered.
There's maybe two inches of *topsoil* over solid clay.

ru: грунт для рассады и комнатных растений
gloss: A light bagged mix used for growing plants in containers.
examples: Pick up a bag of *potting soil* while you're out.
Never use garden dirt where you need *potting soil*.
This *potting soil* holds water way too long.
contrast: Uncountable: a bag of *potting soil*, never a potting soil. The British call it potting compost.

gloss: A liquid or powder added to water to feed potted plants.
examples: Add a capful of *plant food* every other watering.
The *plant food* is under the sink.
Too much *plant food* will burn the roots.

gloss: Light brown decayed moss mixed into soil to hold moisture.
examples: Work some *peat moss* into that sandy bed.
A bale of *peat moss* costs about fifteen dollars.
*Peat moss* makes the soil more acidic.

gloss: Ground animal bone used as a slow fertilizer, especially for bulbs.
examples: Put a spoonful of *bone meal* in each hole.
*Bone meal* is what my grandmother swore by for tulips.
The dog dug up everything I treated with *bone meal*.

gloss: White volcanic granules mixed into soil to keep it loose and draining.
examples: Those little white specks in the mix are *perlite*.
Add a couple handfuls of *perlite* for the cuttings.
*Perlite* keeps the pot from staying soggy.

gloss: A light flaky mineral mixed into soil to hold water and air.
examples: Cover the seeds with a thin layer of *vermiculite*.
*Vermiculite* holds water better than perlite does.
The starting mix is peat and *vermiculite*.

gloss: Crumbly dark material made of leaves that have rotted down.
examples: Two years in a pile turns leaves into *leaf mold*.
He digs *leaf mold* into every bed in the fall.
*Leaf mold* smells like the floor of a forest.
contrast: American *mold*, British mould — same word, different spelling.

gloss: Small pieces of chopped wood spread on paths and around plants.
examples: The tree crew dumped a pile of *wood chips* for free.
We put *wood chips* down the whole side path.
*Wood chips* break down slower than bark.
contrast: Used in the plural as a material: some *wood chips*, not a wood chip.

gloss: The cut grass left behind after mowing a lawn.
examples: Leave the *grass clippings* on the lawn as fertilizer.
He bagged the *grass clippings* for the compost.
Wet *grass clippings* clog the mower.
contrast: Always plural: the *grass clippings*, never a grass clipping.

gloss: Seed spread on bare ground to grow a lawn.
examples: Throw some *grass seed* on that bald spot.
The *grass seed* won't come up until it warms up.
Birds ate half the *grass seed* I put down.

gloss: Grass sold in strips with the soil and roots attached, laid to make an instant lawn.
examples: They laid *sod* over the whole front yard in one day.
New *sod* has to be watered every morning.
It's cheaper than *sod*, but seed takes a season.
contrast: Americans lay *sod*; the British call the same thing turf.

gloss: Rich crumbly soil that is a good balance of sand, silt, and clay.
examples: That whole valley is deep black *loam*.
Vegetables do best in *loam*.
Years of compost turned the clay into decent *loam*.

gloss: Fine soil particles, finer than sand, left behind by moving water.
examples: The flood left an inch of *silt* on the garden.
*Silt* packs down hard when it dries.
Good soil has sand, clay, and *silt* in it.

gloss: The dark rotted matter in soil that makes it rich.
examples: Forest soil is full of *humus*.
Compost adds *humus* to a tired bed.
The *humus* is what holds the water.
contrast: Not *hummus*, the chickpea dip: HYOO-muhs for the soil, HUM-uhs for the food.

gloss: A low spreading plant grown to cover bare soil.
examples: Creeping thyme makes a nice *ground cover* between the stones.
We need a *ground cover* for that slope.
Most shade-tolerant *ground covers* spread slowly.

gloss: A small paper envelope of seeds sold for planting.
examples: The *seed packet* says thin to six inches.
I have a shoebox full of old *seed packets*.
Check the date on the back of the *seed packet*.

gloss: A shallow plastic tray with small cells for starting seedlings.
examples: The peppers are up in the *seed tray* already.
Put the *seed tray* on the windowsill.
She washes and reuses the *seed trays* every year.

gloss: A mailed or online listing of seeds and plants a company sells.
examples: The *seed catalogs* start showing up in January.
He circles half the *seed catalog* and orders three things.
That *seed catalog* has forty kinds of tomatoes.
contrast: American *catalog*, British catalogue.

gloss: A patch of finely worked soil prepared for sowing seed.
examples: Rake the *seedbed* smooth before you sow.
A crusted *seedbed* keeps seedlings from breaking through.
He prepares his *seedbeds* the week before planting.

gloss: A long shallow groove cut in soil for planting or watering.
examples: Draw a *furrow* with the corner of the hoe.
Drop the peas along the *furrow* about two inches apart.
The water runs down the *furrows* to the far end.

gloss: A new stem or growth coming out of a plant.
examples: Green *shoots* are already coming up along the fence.
Pinch off that *shoot* growing out of the trunk.
The first *shoots* appear about two weeks after planting.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *chute*, the sliding channel.

gloss: A piece of stem cut from a plant and rooted to grow a new one.
examples: She rooted a *cutting* from her mother's rose bush.
Take *cuttings* about four inches long.
Half the *cuttings* took, half rotted.

gloss: A shoot joined onto another plant so the two grow as one.
examples: You can see the *graft* right above the soil line.
The *graft* never took, so he tried again in spring.
All the *grafts* on that apple tree are different varieties.

gloss: A thick underground stem that stores food, like a potato.
examples: Dig the *tubers* after the tops die back.
Each *tuber* should have at least one eye.
Store the *tubers* somewhere cool and dark.
contrast: Americans say TOO-bur; the British say TYOO-bur.

gloss: A stem that creeps sideways underground and sends up new plants.
examples: Mint spreads by *rhizomes*, so keep it in a pot.
Split the *rhizome* with a sharp knife.
Those *rhizomes* went straight under the sidewalk.
contrast: The h is silent: rh- is just R, as in rhyme.

gloss: A small shoot or twig cut from a plant, usually an herb.
examples: Add a *sprig* of rosemary to the pan.
She cut a few *sprigs* of mint for the pitcher.
One *sprig* of thyme is plenty.

gloss: A thin curling growth a climbing plant uses to hold on.
examples: The pea *tendrils* have grabbed the string already.
A *tendril* had wrapped itself around the railing.
Cucumber *tendrils* will pull down a weak trellis.

gloss: All the roots of a plant taken together.
examples: Bamboo has a *root system* that will wreck a patio.
The tree's *root system* goes out farther than its branches.
Shallow *root systems* dry out fast.

gloss: The mass of roots and soil that comes out with a plant when it is moved.
examples: Loosen the *root ball* before you set it in the hole.
The *root ball* was completely dried out.
Dig a hole twice as wide as the *root ball*.

gloss: A plant that dies back in winter and comes up again year after year.
examples: Hostas are the easiest *perennial* I know.
She filled the shady bed with *perennials*.
That *perennial* has come back for nine years.

gloss: A plant that grows, flowers, and dies all in one season.
examples: I put a flat of *annuals* in the window boxes every May.
Marigold is an *annual*, so it won't come back.
*Annuals* bloom all summer if you keep them watered.

gloss: A plant that grows leaves the first year and flowers the second.
examples: Foxglove is a *biennial*, so be patient.
*Biennials* are worth the wait.
That *biennial* finally bloomed this June.
contrast: *Biennial* means every two years; *biannual* means twice a year.

gloss: A plant bred from two different varieties.
examples: This tomato is a *hybrid* bred for disease resistance.
Seeds saved from a *hybrid* rarely come out the same.
Most of the corn in the store is from *hybrids*.

gloss: A named kind of plant within a species.
examples: That *variety* ripens two weeks earlier.
The nursery carries about ten *varieties* of apple.
Ask for a *variety* that does well in heat.

gloss: Green leaves and plants taken together.
examples: The porch is buried in *greenery* by July.
She added some *greenery* to the arrangement.
There's not much *greenery* on that side of the house.

gloss: A planting of bushes growing together.
examples: The ball went into the *shrubbery*.
He trimmed the *shrubbery* along the walk.
Birds nest in that *shrubbery* every spring.

gloss: A line of bushes and small trees growing along a field or road.
examples: Rabbits live in the *hedgerow* behind the barn.
The old *hedgerows* mark where the fences used to be.
A *hedgerow* blocks the wind better than a fence.

gloss: A prickly bush of the blackberry or raspberry kind.
examples: The back corner is nothing but *brambles*.
He cut a path through the *bramble* with a machete.
Those *brambles* will take over if you let them.

gloss: A weed with hairy leaves that sting the skin.
examples: I grabbed a *nettle* and my hand burned for an hour.
*Nettles* love rich damp soil.
Wear gloves — that whole bed is full of *nettles*.

gloss: A prickly weed with purple flowers and seeds that blow away.
examples: Pull the *thistle* before it goes to seed.
*Thistles* come right back if you leave the root.
One *thistle* turns into fifty by next summer.
contrast: The t is silent: THIS-uhl, like whistle.

gloss: A big leafy tree planted to give shade.
examples: Plant a *shade tree* on the west side of the house.
The *shade tree* out front drops leaves for a month.
Those *shade trees* cut our cooling bill in half.

gloss: A machine that blows a strong stream of air to clear leaves.
examples: Somebody fires up a *leaf blower* at seven every morning.
The battery *leaf blower* is a lot quieter.
Half the town runs *leaf blowers* in October.

gloss: A powered tool with a long toothed blade for shaping hedges.
examples: Run the *hedge trimmer* along the top to even it out.
The *hedge trimmer* is in the shed with the extension cord.
Cordless *hedge trimmers* have gotten pretty good.

gloss: A machine that cuts grass and weeds with a spinning nylon line.
examples: Use the *string trimmer* along the fence line.
The *string trimmer* is out of line again.
Both *string trimmers* need new spools.
contrast: Most Americans call it a *weed whacker* or a weed eater in everyday speech.

gloss: The everyday name for a string trimmer.
examples: Can I borrow your *weed whacker* this weekend?
He went after the ditch with a *weed whacker*.
The *weed whacker* won't start when it's cold.

gloss: A hand tool with two curved blades for cutting small branches.
examples: Hand me the *pruning shears* — this cane is done.
The *pruning shears* need sharpening.
Wipe the *pruning shears* with alcohol between plants.
contrast: Always plural, like scissors: a pair of *pruning shears*, even though Russian секатор is singular.

gloss: A small curved saw for cutting branches too thick for shears.
examples: That limb needs a *pruning saw*.
A folding *pruning saw* fits right in your back pocket.
Both *pruning saws* cut on the pull stroke.

gloss: A cutting tool with two long handles for thick branches.
examples: Get the *loppers* — the shears won't go through that.
The *loppers* are hanging in the garage.
These *loppers* will take a branch an inch and a half thick.
contrast: Always plural: a pair of *loppers*, never a lopper.

gloss: A long-handled fork with long thin tines for lifting hay or straw.
examples: He turned the pile with a *pitchfork*.
The *pitchfork* is leaning against the barn.
Two *pitchforks* and a wheelbarrow, and we were done.
contrast: Russian вилы is plural, but one tool is a *pitchfork*, singular.

gloss: A short sturdy fork with flat tines for digging and loosening soil.
examples: Work the compost in with a *garden fork*.
A *garden fork* is better than a shovel in heavy clay.
He bent two *garden forks* on those rocks.

gloss: A tool with curved prongs for breaking up and stirring the top of the soil.
examples: Run a *cultivator* through the row to kill the small weeds.
The hand *cultivator* is perfect for container soil.
Both *cultivators* are hanging by the door.

gloss: A gas or electric machine with turning blades that chops up garden soil.
examples: We rented a *tiller* for the new bed.
The *tiller* bounced right off that hardpan.
Small *tillers* work fine for a raised bed.

gloss: A lawn mower with a seat that the operator drives.
examples: You need a *riding mower* for two acres.
The *riding mower* is in the shed under a tarp.
Used *riding mowers* go fast around here.

gloss: A tool or machine that cuts a clean line where a lawn meets a walk or bed.
examples: Run the *edger* along the driveway last.
A sharp *edger* makes the whole yard look finished.
They sell manual *edgers* for about thirty dollars.

gloss: A tool with a long curved blade and a long handle for cutting tall grass by hand.
examples: He still cuts the back field with a *scythe*.
A *scythe* has to be sharpened every twenty minutes.
Two old *scythes* were hanging in the barn.
contrast: Spelled scythe but said SYTH — the c is silent, and it rhymes with writhe.

gloss: A short curved blade with a handle, used to cut grass or grain by hand.
examples: She cleared the weeds with a *sickle*.
A *sickle* is faster than pulling by hand.
The old *sickles* still hang on the shed wall.

gloss: A tank with a pump and nozzle for spraying plants.
examples: Fill the *sprayer* and go after the aphids.
The *sprayer* clogs if you don't rinse it.
He keeps separate *sprayers* for weed killer and for feed.

gloss: A flat frame of crossed strips that a climbing plant grows up.
examples: Tie the vine loosely to the *trellis*.
The *trellis* blew over in the first storm.
Both *trellises* are covered in clematis by June.

gloss: A pointed stick driven into the ground to support a plant.
examples: Drive a *stake* in next to each tomato.
The wind snapped the *stake* right off.
We ran out of *stakes* halfway down the row.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *steak*, the piece of meat.

gloss: A decorative container that plants are grown in.
examples: There's a big *planter* on each side of the door.
That ceramic *planter* has no drainage hole.
She filled the *planters* with geraniums.

gloss: A container of flowers hung from a hook or bracket.
examples: A *hanging basket* dries out twice as fast as a pot.
She hung a *hanging basket* on each porch post.
The store had *hanging baskets* on sale for Mother's Day.

gloss: A long shallow container of plants fixed under a window.
examples: The *window box* is full of petunias.
He built a cedar *window box* for the kitchen.
The *window boxes* have to be watered every evening.

gloss: A low box with a clear lid that protects young plants from frost.
examples: The lettuce lives in the *cold frame* until April.
Prop the *cold frame* open on warm days.
He built two *cold frames* out of old storm windows.

gloss: A waist-high table used for filling pots and working with plants.
examples: The *potting bench* is buried under empty containers.
He built a *potting bench* out of scrap lumber.
Most *potting benches* have a shelf underneath.

gloss: A small outbuilding where tools and supplies are kept.
examples: The mower lives in the *garden shed*.
There's a wasp nest in the *garden shed* again.
Both *garden sheds* need new roofs.

gloss: An electric lamp that gives plants the light they need indoors.
examples: Start the seedlings under a *grow light* in February.
The *grow light* hangs a few inches over the tray.
LED *grow lights* barely use any power.

gloss: A large container that catches roof runoff for watering plants.
examples: The *rain barrel* fills up in one good storm.
He put a *rain barrel* under each downspout.
Two *rain barrels* get us through most dry spells.
contrast: Americans say *rain barrel*; the British say water butt.

gloss: Light wire mesh with small holes, used to fence plants off from animals.
examples: Put *chicken wire* around the beans or the rabbits will get them.
A roll of *chicken wire* is about twenty dollars.
The *chicken wire* is stapled to the fence posts.
contrast: Uncountable: a roll of *chicken wire*, never a chicken wire.

gloss: An arched garden structure that vines are trained over.
examples: They got married under a rose *arbor*.
The *arbor* marks the entrance to the back garden.
Both *arbors* need repainting.
contrast: American *arbor*, British arbour.

gloss: An open frame of posts and crossbeams that shades a walk or patio.
examples: Grapevines cover the whole *pergola* by August.
They built a *pergola* over the back patio.
Cedar *pergolas* hold up better than pine.
contrast: The stress is on the first syllable: PUR-guh-luh.

gloss: A flat stone set in the ground to walk on.
examples: One *stepping stone* has sunk about two inches.
The *stepping stones* lead from the gate to the porch.
Set each *stepping stone* on a bed of sand.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: Flat split stone used for paths and patios.
examples: They laid a *flagstone* path from the driveway.
One *flagstone* cracked over the winter.
Moss grows in the gaps between the *flagstones*.

gloss: A low fence of upright pointed boards with gaps between them.
examples: A white *picket fence* runs across the front.
The *picket fence* needs painting every few years.
Roses grow along both *picket fences*.

gloss: An upright piece of wood or metal set in the ground to hold a fence.
examples: Set the *fence post* in concrete.
That *fence post* has rotted right at the soil line.
We dug holes for eight *fence posts*.

gloss: A low wall built to hold back soil on a slope.
examples: They put in a stone *retaining wall* to level the yard.
The *retaining wall* is starting to bow out.
Two low *retaining walls* turned the hill into terraces.

gloss: A border of brick, stone, or plastic set along a bed or path.
examples: Brick *edging* keeps the mulch off the lawn.
He put plastic *edging* around every bed.
The *edging* has heaved up over the winter.

gloss: A small statue of a bearded man used as a yard ornament.
examples: There's a *garden gnome* under the birdbath.
Somebody stole the *garden gnome* off the porch.
She has eleven *garden gnomes* and counting.
contrast: The g in *gnome* is silent: NOHM.

ru: декоративный водоём или фонтан в саду
gloss: A pond, fountain, or small waterfall built into a garden.
examples: They put in a small *water feature* by the patio.
The *water feature* runs on a little pump.
*Water features* attract more birds than a feeder does.

gloss: A store that sells plants, soil, and garden supplies.
examples: The *garden center* is packed every Saturday in May.
I got the tomato starts at the *garden center*.
Both *garden centers* in town close for the winter.
contrast: American *center*, British centre.

gloss: A small planting of cooking herbs.
examples: The *herb garden* is right outside the kitchen door.
Mint took over half the *herb garden*.
*Herb gardens* do fine in pots on a balcony.
contrast: In American English the h in *herb* is silent: URB gar-duhn, not HURB.

gloss: A small garden of vegetables and herbs grown for the household.
examples: She keeps a *kitchen garden* right off the back steps.
A *kitchen garden* pays for itself in a season.
The old farmhouse had two *kitchen gardens*.

gloss: A garden of stones planted with small tough plants that like dry soil.
examples: The slope became a *rock garden*.
Nothing but weeds grows in that *rock garden* now.
*Rock gardens* need almost no watering.

gloss: A shared piece of land divided into plots that people rent to grow food.
examples: We got a plot at the *community garden* on Elm.
The *community garden* has a waiting list two years long.
The city runs four *community gardens*.

gloss: A public garden where many kinds of plants are grown and labeled.
examples: The *botanical garden* is free on Tuesdays.
We spent the afternoon at the *botanical garden*.
Most big cities have *botanical gardens*.

gloss: A park where trees are grown and studied.
examples: The *arboretum* has a hundred kinds of maple.
We walk the *arboretum* every fall for the color.
University *arboretums* are usually open to the public.
contrast: The plural is *arboretums* or, more formally, arboreta.

gloss: A natural skill for making plants grow well.
examples: She has a real *green thumb*.
I do not have a *green thumb* — I've killed three cactuses.
It takes a *green thumb* to keep orchids blooming.
contrast: The b in *thumb* is silent, and the British say green fingers instead.

gloss: The stretch of the year warm enough for plants to grow.
examples: Our *growing season* runs from mid-May to early October.
A short *growing season* rules out melons.
The last two *growing seasons* have been dry.

gloss: The time of year when things are put in the ground.
examples: The nursery hires extra people for *planting season*.
Fall is the better *planting season* for trees.
We've missed two *planting seasons* in a row.

gloss: A numbered region based on how cold the winter gets, used to pick plants.
examples: We're in *hardiness zone* six.
Check the *hardiness zone* on the tag before you buy.
The map splits the country into thirteen *hardiness zones*.

gloss: The practice of planting different crops in a bed each year.
examples: *Crop rotation* keeps disease from building up in the soil.
He uses a four-year *crop rotation*.
Without *crop rotation* the tomatoes get blight every summer.

gloss: A crop grown to protect and feed bare soil rather than to be eaten.
examples: Sow a *cover crop* of rye after the last harvest.
The *cover crop* gets turned under in spring.
Clover and vetch are the usual *cover crops* here.

gloss: The supplying of water to land or plants through pipes or channels.
examples: Nothing grows out there without *irrigation*.
The *irrigation* runs on a timer at dawn.
They ran *irrigation* to the far end of the field.

gloss: A system of thin tubes that drips water slowly right at the roots.
examples: *Drip irrigation* cut our water bill way down.
He put *drip irrigation* in all four raised beds.
With *drip irrigation* the leaves stay dry.

gloss: A porous hose that lets water seep out along its whole length.
examples: Snake a *soaker hose* down the middle of the row.
The *soaker hose* is buried under the mulch.
Two *soaker hoses* cover the whole bed.

gloss: A set of buried pipes and pop-up heads that waters a lawn automatically.
examples: The *sprinkler system* comes on at five a.m.
We had the *sprinkler system* blown out before the freeze.
New *sprinkler systems* run off a phone app.

gloss: An outdoor tap that a garden hose screws onto.
examples: Hook the hose up to the *spigot* on the side of the house.
The *spigot* drips no matter how hard you crank it.
There are *spigots* front and back.
contrast: Americans say *spigot* or faucet; the British say tap.

gloss: The way water flows away from soil or a container.
examples: That corner has terrible *drainage*.
Gravel in the bottom improves *drainage*.
Most plants die from bad *drainage*, not from cold.

gloss: The pulling of small plugs of soil out of a lawn to let in air and water.
examples: The lawn is due for *aeration* this fall.
*Aeration* helps most on hard clay.
They charge about a hundred dollars for *aeration*.

gloss: The removal of faded flowers so a plant keeps blooming.
examples: A little *deadheading* keeps the petunias going all summer.
She does the *deadheading* with her morning coffee.
Without *deadheading* they set seed and quit.

gloss: The pulling out of extra seedlings so the rest have room.
examples: The carrots need *thinning* or you'll get nothing but tops.
*Thinning* feels wasteful, but it doubles the crop.
Do the *thinning* when the plants are two inches tall.

gloss: The growing of new plants from seeds, cuttings, or division.
examples: *Propagation* by cuttings is the fastest way to fill a bed.
The class covers seed starting and *propagation*.
She keeps a whole shelf for *propagation*.

gloss: The sprouting of a seed into a young plant.
examples: *Germination* takes seven to ten days.
Cold soil slows *germination* way down.
The packet promises ninety percent *germination*.

gloss: The carrying of pollen to a flower so it can make fruit or seed.
examples: No bees, no *pollination*, no squash.
You can do the *pollination* by hand with a small brush.
Wind handles the *pollination* for corn.

gloss: The process by which green plants make food out of light, air, and water.
examples: Leaves in deep shade barely do any *photosynthesis*.
*Photosynthesis* slows down when it gets too hot.
Dust on the leaves cuts down *photosynthesis*.

gloss: The work of preparing soil and raising plants on it.
examples: That field has been under *cultivation* for a century.
Roses need more *cultivation* than most people expect.
The book covers the *cultivation* of fruit trees.

gloss: The science and business of growing garden plants.
examples: She studied *horticulture* at the state college.
*Horticulture* is a big employer in this county.
He came to *horticulture* after twenty years in banking.

gloss: A trained expert in growing plants.
examples: The city *horticulturist* picked the street trees.
Ask a *horticulturist* before you cut that back.
Two *horticulturists* run the whole display garden.

gloss: Someone whose job is designing and taking care of yards and grounds.
examples: We hired a *landscaper* to redo the front.
The *landscaper* said the soil had to be replaced.
*Landscapers* are booked solid all spring.

gloss: A person who maintains the lawns and grounds of a large property.
examples: The *groundskeeper* has the field cut by six in the morning.
Talk to the *groundskeeper* about the sprinklers.
The campus employs six *groundskeepers*.

ru: арборист, специалист по уходу за деревьями
gloss: A specialist in the care and pruning of trees.
examples: Get an *arborist* to look at that split trunk.
The *arborist* said the oak could be saved.
Certified *arborists* charge more, and they're worth it.
contrast: Americans hire an *arborist*; the British often say tree surgeon.

gloss: A plant disease that makes leaves and stems turn brown and die.
examples: *Blight* took every tomato we had by August.
Copper spray slows the *blight* down a little.
Wet summers here always mean *blight*.
contrast: The gh is silent: BLYTE, rhyming with light.

gloss: A white or gray fungus that coats leaves in damp weather.
examples: The squash leaves are covered in *mildew*.
*Mildew* shows up every year once the nights cool off.
Space the plants out and you'll get less *mildew*.
contrast: Americans say MIL-doo; the British say MIL-dyoo.

gloss: Soft decay in a plant caused by too much moisture or disease.
examples: The bulbs sat in wet soil and went to *rot*.
Root *rot* killed both of my houseplants.
Cut away the *rot* and repot what's left.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A chemical used to kill unwanted plants.
examples: They sprayed *herbicide* along the fence line.
That *herbicide* will kill the grass too.
New *herbicides* break down faster in the soil.
contrast: Many Americans drop the h and say UR-buh-syde, the way they say *herb*.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A chemical used to stop fungus from spreading on plants.
examples: Spray a *fungicide* before the spots show up.
The *fungicide* has to be reapplied after rain.
There are organic *fungicides* that work almost as well.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A product sprayed on unwanted plants to kill them.
examples: Don't use *weed killer* that close to the vegetables.
The *weed killer* took three days to work.
Most *weed killers* won't touch a dandelion root.

gloss: An unusually large harvest.
examples: We had a *bumper crop* of zucchini and gave most of it away.
The wet spring gave everybody a *bumper crop*.
Two *bumper crops* in a row is almost unheard of.

gloss: The amount a plant or plot produces.
examples: The *yield* was down about a third this year.
Pinching the tips gives you a bigger *yield*.
*Yields* drop off fast once it turns dry.

gloss: A tree kept tiny in a shallow pot by careful pruning.
examples: His *bonsai* is older than he is.
A *bonsai* has to be watered almost every day.
She keeps four *bonsai* on the windowsill.
contrast: The plural is usually *bonsai*, unchanged.

gloss: A shrub clipped into a decorative shape.
examples: There's a *topiary* shaped like a rabbit by the gate.
The *topiaries* get trimmed twice a summer.
One overgrown *topiary* is just a bush again.

gloss: Growing plants in water and nutrients instead of soil.
examples: The lettuce at that farm is all *hydroponics*.
*Hydroponics* uses far less water than field growing.
He got into *hydroponics* to grow greens in the basement.
contrast: Ends in -s but takes a singular verb: *hydroponics* is expensive to set up.

gloss: A row of trees or a fence planted to block the wind.
examples: They planted a row of spruce as a *windbreak*.
The *windbreak* keeps the snow off the driveway.
*Windbreaks* make a real difference out on the plains.

gloss: A panel of thin strips crossed in a diamond pattern, used for screens and climbing plants.
examples: He nailed a *lattice* under the porch to hide the crawl space.
The clematis has covered the whole *lattice*.
Vinyl *lattices* don't rot the way wood ones do.

gloss: A light cloth laid over plants to hold in warmth and keep insects off.
examples: Throw a *row cover* over the beans before the frost.
The *row cover* is held down with bricks.
*Row covers* have to come off once the plants flower.
contrast: *Row* here rhymes with go, not with cow.
